book: 202 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason

chapters.file: ch25 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Kempner reads the comic through Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism': with God and the old world gone, survivors like Rick, Michonne, and Dale must create their own values, while characters who cling to pre-apocalypse essences (Hershel keeping his zombified son in the barn, Shane waiting for the government) bring death on themselves. Rick's hospital awakening is treated as an existential rebirth in which his cop uniform is an 'essence precedes existence' trap, and Carl shooting Shane (and later Ben in 'Fear the Hunters') shows children making free choices outside conventional morality. The chapter concludes the series is 'sternly optimistic' because total freedom, not zombification, is what defines the humans: 'in a world ruled by the dead, we are forced to finally start living.'

chapters.file: ch26 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Round argues modern zombie fiction's real horror is humanity, reading The Walking Dead existentially: Rick builds meaning through self-imposed missions, revises his morals ('You kill, you die' then killing Dexter anyway), and demands in his 'We ARE the walking dead' speech (Issue #24) that the group admit their new nature instead of hiding in bad faith behind old rules. Kierkegaard's Abraham illuminates Rick's suspension of universal ethics, while Sergeant Abraham Ford's confession 'No. I did what I wanted to do' models owning one's choices, and his angst after Eugene's lie shows the cost of projected meaning collapsing. Camus supplies persistence against the absurd (suicides like Jim, Jacqui, and Carol exert the only control left), and Adorno's Marxist critique frames the Governor's Woodbury as an inauthentic hierarchy that denies its people authentic choice.

chapters.file: ch27 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Greeley argues the zombie embodies a specifically modern fear of losing our humanity: walkers are persons stripped of the potential Aristotle and Aquinas made the measure of human worth, which is why Rick uniquely eulogizes the walkers he puts down ('I'm sorry this happened to you'). Following Aries, he traces modern death anxiety to the split of faith from reason and reads the CDC arc ('TS-19') as science offering only a self-destruct quick death where Jacqui's 'wrath of God' guess at least offers meaning. Rousseau's claim that civilization corrupts explains the survivors' return to the woods, where pizza-deliverer Glenn's heroics and the 'kingpin' Guillermo protecting nursing-home patients show the apocalypse can bring out the best in us while the Bradbury's Sale storefront and trampled Walmart worker hint we were already the walking dead.

chapters.file: ch28 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
ch29 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Hinzmann and Arp ask whether walkers can be morally harmed, ranking perceptual, reasoning, and conscious minds and placing zombies at shark level on the evidence of Dr. Jenner's fMRI ('TS-19') showing only the brain stem reactivates. Surveying anthropocentric views (Michonne's chained pet-walkers as guard-dog tools), Singer's expanding circle, Leopold's land ethic, and Naess's deep ecology, they conclude that even utilitarians could demand a zombie preserve on the model of Hershel's barn of 'sick people', which Shane's barn massacre in 'Pretty Much Dead Already' destroys. Kant's point that cruelty to animals corrodes our humanity explains why the Governor's death-match arena, his torture of Rick and Michonne, and his chained zombie daughter mark him, not the walkers, as the true moral monster.

chapters.file: ch30 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Allaire defends the thesis that the only good walker is a dead one: walkers fall outside Kant's moral community because, as purely sensuous beings driven by instinct, they cannot plan ahead (Glenn's 'Vatos' heist, the walker-guts camouflage in 'Guts'), communicate, or reflect, and so can have no duties and no rights. Act-utilitarian weighing shows killing any walker is beneficial, and even Regan's respect principle does not apply; the chapter runs Mary Anne Warren's personhood criteria to show walkers lack consciousness, reasoning, and self-awareness. Our hesitation before walkers like Morgan's wife or Leon Basset is irrational projection onto beings no longer the persons we loved, so Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' is mercy for a fate, not respect for a right-holder.

chapters.file: ch31 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Barkman distinguishes the self-evident natural law (general beneficence, special preference for family, piety to parents as Confucius taught, duties to the weak) from derivative rules like 'do not steal' and from positive law, concluding that Andrea's mermaid necklace looting question in 'Guts' is really about whether natural law still binds when the state has collapsed. He argues it does: Andrea's necklace is unowned and free to take, Rick taking surplus food from Andrea would be justified by equal claims to survival, and Carol's 'we can make new rules' polygamy proposal fails because the natural law is prior to any government. The cannibal hunters of Issues #61-66 show what happens without virtue and Aristotle's practical wisdom for weighing conflicting principles, and walkers are bad but not evil, while a Governor-like human who ignores the natural law 'reduces himself to the level of a walker.'

chapters.file: ch32 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Rard tests whether any morality survives the apocalypse with an objective basis: Plato's Forms fail to capture changing facts (Hannah the bicycle girl decaying from mom to walker) and white lies, and Aristotle's function-based virtue ethics proves too relative and luck-dependent for survivors like Rick (rashness at Carl's shooting) and Shane (courage fetching supplies, rage at the barn). Nietzsche then supplies the frame: Hershel's barn of pitied 'sick people' is Christian slave morality that guilts the strong, and Shane's sacrifice of Otis and forcing open of the barn doors grope toward a master morality 'for the Walker Age' without ever achieving nobility. Rick alone approaches the higher type, refusing to judge Lori's affair, insisting the baby be born, and embracing the post-walker world as one he would choose again.

chapters.file: ch33 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Moosa treats Kirkman's world as a moral laboratory: the apocalypse approximates Hobbes's state of nature ('solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'), yet Rick's search for his family shows survivors import morality into it, and Carl's killing of Shane is judged by reasoning rather than the act of killing itself. Taking Camus's claim that suicide is the only serious philosophical problem, the chapter argues the survivors' best justification for continuing is reducing others' suffering, and consistency then imposes the same duty on comfortable readers to help real-world sufferers rather than reserving aid for photogenic disasters. It concludes that Glenn and Maggie's wish to conceive at the prison is the worst thing survivors can do, since non-existent children cannot suffer while existing orphans (like the children Andrea and Dale adopted) have prior moral claims, an argument that applies to couples in our world too.

chapters.file: ch34 - The Walking Dead and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Yuen argues cannibalism is not automatically wrong: both utilitarian and Kantian frameworks permit eating the already-dead in a genuine survival situation like the Andes crash of Alive, since corpses lose no happiness and lack the rational nature owed dignity. But Chris's hunters in 'Fear the Hunters' become moral monsters because they kill to eat (murdering their own children, amputating and eating the still-living Dale to prolong his terror), which neither maximizes utility nor treats persons as ends, and Chris's 'we had no choice' excuse fails because starving is not a license to murder when one could befriend other survivors, eat walkers, or starve. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended on Kantian grounds of deserved punishment: applying Chris's own maxim ('if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris') as a universal law.

holes.name: Facticity
holes.what: The existentialist term for the given facts of one's situation and past, which are part of the self but whose value and power the free individual chooses.
holes.why: Chapter 26 has a dedicated section on facticity to explain Rick's claim that 'We became what we are': the group must own its past violence without letting it trap them, and neither denying nor being determined by the past is inauthentic.

holes.name: Personhood Criteria (Warren's five criteria)
holes.what: Mary Anne Warren's five criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, capacity to communicate, self-awareness) for deciding which beings count as persons with moral rights.
holes.why: Chapter 30's entire case that walkers have no duties and hence no rights rests on checking walkers against Warren's personhood criteria, and the taxonomy has no personhood-criteria entry.

holes.name: Antinatalism
holes.what: The view that procreation is morally wrong because non-existent children cannot suffer and cannot consent, while existing children (e.g. orphans available for adoption) have prior claims on parental care.
holes.why: Chapter 33's central argument is that Glenn and Maggie act immorally by trying to conceive at the prison and that couples in our world should adopt rather than create children, an antinatalist case the taxonomy cannot tag.
